It will make the water thick.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write it at the top of the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Glowing Fog test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Pour 500 millilitres of water into the jar. 2. Draw centimetre marks along the card. 3. Lower the card, black patch first, to the bottom. 4. Write 0 teaspoons and the depth in the first row.
flow.say: First the clear water. Lower the card slowly. Can you see the black patch all the way to the bottom?
flow.kid: Pour in the water. Lower the card. Can you see the black patch at the bottom?
flow.parent: In clear water you should see the black patch right down to the bottom. If the jar is deeper than the card, write the deepest depth you can read and say 'to the bottom'.

check.q: Why do we test clear water first?
options: To have a starting point to compare with
check.why: A starting point shows what normal looks like. Without it, we could not say that the milk made any change. Picking 'to make the card wet' mixes up a side effect with the purpose.

flow.context: In this step, you test clear water with no milk. This is the starting point.

flow.do: 1. Stir in a quarter teaspoon of milk. 2. Lower the card until the black patch just vanishes. 3. Read the depth on the card. 4. Do it again to check. 5. Add more milk to reach a total of half, one, two and four teaspoons. Read the depth each time.
flow.say: Stir in the milk and wait for the swirls to settle. Lower the card until the black patch just disappears. What depth is that? Check it twice.
flow.kid: Stir in milk. Lower the card until the black patch vanishes. Read the depth.

ask.q: What happens to the depth where you can see the patch as you add more milk?
good: The cloud hides the patch sooner.

flow.parent: If the patch vanishes at once with the first quarter spoon, start again with 5 drops. If you can still see to the bottom after four spoons, the milk may be very thin, so add more. The numbers will vary with your jar and light, and that is fine.

check.q: You add more milk. Where does the black patch vanish?
options: Nearer the top of the jar
check.why: More milk scatters more light, so light from the patch is lost sooner. You can see only a short way into thick cloud. Picking deeper down would mean the cloud had cleared, which is the opposite of what the milk does.

flow.context: In this step, you add milk bit by bit and find how deep you can see each time.

flow.do: 1. Make the room as dark as you can. 2. Stand the jar with a lot of milk on a lit torch lying face up. 3. Look at the glow from the side. 4. Then look down into the jar from a slant, not straight at the torch. 5. Write what you see.
flow.say: In the dark, look at the glow from the side. Is there a sharp edge, or does it fade? What colour is it? Then look down from a slant. Is the colour the same?
flow.kid: Make the room dark. Look at the glow from the side. Does it have a sharp edge?

ask.q: Where would you say the top of the glow is?
good: It fades slowly, so there is no sharp top.
It is where I stop seeing the light.

flow.parent: Do not look straight at the torch's bulb from above, as it can dazzle. The glow looks bluish from the side and yellow-orange when you look down through it, as the sky is blue and a sunset is orange. This is the same effect.

check.q: Where is the top edge of the glow?
options: It is a wall that stops the light
It is where the light has faded so much that we stop seeing it
It is where the torch ends
check.why: The milky water has no wall. The glow only fades as light is scattered away. The edge we see is where there is too little light left for our eyes. The Sun's edge is a little like this.

flow.context: In this step, you look at the milky glow in the dark and ask where its edge is.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what I think, what I saw and why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a cloud has no hard edge, and how far we can see in depends on how thick it is. What I saw: with clear water I saw the patch to the bottom, and with four teaspoons I lost it within a centimetre. Why: the milk scatters light, so light from deeper down cannot reach my eyes.
flow.think: The Sun is a ball of gas. Where might its edge be, and could you put your hand in it if you could get there?
flow.context: In this last step, you say what you found and link it to the Sun.

experiments.title: The Boiling Pot: how the Sun's surface churns
experiments.question: When a pot of water is heated from below, which way does the water move? Does it go round in loops, and how long does one loop take?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the water stay still until it boils, or will it move? If it moves, where will it rise, and where will it sink? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same pan, the same water and the same flame for the whole test. Time three different specks, because one speck can be a fluke. Only the speck changes, so any difference comes from where it is in the pan.
results_table: Where it rose and where it sank

materials.item: a wide steel pan or kadai, about 20 cm across, that you can look into from above
1 litre of water, measured with a jug
half a teaspoon of ground black pepper
a gas stove or an induction plate, run by a grown-up
a clock or phone with a seconds timer
a stool or step so your child can look from the side, at arm's length from the pan

experiments.safety: A grown-up runs the stove and holds the pan. Keep a low flame. Keep your child back by an arm's length. Turn the pan handle inwards. Tie back long hair and do not touch the pan or the steam. Switch off the heat when you finish and leave the pan to cool before you move it.

schedule.what: When a pot of water is heated from below, which way does the water move? Does it go round in loops, and how long does one loop take?

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the pan from above, with arrows showing which way the specks went. Mark where they rose and where they sank.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you warm a pan of water and watch pepper specks to see how hot water moves. The Sun's surface moves in a similar way.

setup.art: A wide steel pan of water on a stove with a low flame and half a teaspoon of pepper sprinkled evenly on top, seen from above.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up puts the pan on a low flame. Sprinkle pepper evenly on the water.

setup.art: A child on a stool, an arm's length from the pan, watching specks and holding a timer.
setup.caption: 2. Watch from above, at arm's length. Pick a speck and follow it.

setup.art: The pan seen from above with arrows: specks rising in the middle, moving out along the top, and sinking at the edge.
setup.caption: 3. Draw arrows to show where the specks rose and where they sank.

flow.do: Show your child the pan, the water and the pepper. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: We will warm this water slowly and sprinkle pepper on it. Will the water stay still, or will it move before it boils? If it moves, where? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. Will the water move? Where? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Where in the pan do you think the water will move first?
good: In the middle, because it is hottest.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Boiling Pot test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up pours in the water and puts the pan on a low flame. Wait until you see steam and tiny bubbles on the pan floor, but before boiling. Sprinkle the pepper evenly on top.
flow.say: I will put the pan on a low flame. We wait until the water is hot but not boiling. Then we sprinkle the pepper. Stay back.
flow.kid: A grown-up heats the water on low. Wait for steam. Then sprinkle the pepper.
flow.parent: Do not let the water boil hard, because big bubbles hide the slow loops. If the specks all sink and nothing moves, wait another minute and look again. A very low flame works best. The water should look hot, with steam rising, but not bubbling over.

check.q: Why do we warm the water slowly?
options: So we can see the slow loops before big bubbles hide them
check.why: Boiling hard makes big bubbles that hide the quiet loops. Warm water shows the slow rising and sinking. Picking 'to save gas' is a side effect, not the reason.

flow.context: In this step, a grown-up warms the water and you add the pepper.

flow.do: 1. Look into the pan from above. 2. Find where the specks rise, where they spread out and where they sink. 3. Pick one speck and time how long it takes to go round one loop. 4. Do it for three different specks.
flow.say: Look carefully. Where do the specks rise? Where do they go next? Where do they sink? Pick one speck and count the seconds for one whole loop.
flow.kid: Watch the specks. Where do they rise? Where do they sink? Time one loop.

ask.q: What pattern do the specks make?
good: They rise in the middle and sink at the edge.

flow.parent: Usually the specks rise above the hottest part, which is the middle of a gas flame, spread across the top and sink near the edge. If your pan does it the other way round, write that down. It is a real result. A loop may take 5 to 30 seconds.

check.q: Why does the water in the middle rise?
options: It is hotter and lighter than the cooler water around it
It is heavier than the water around it
check.why: Hot water spreads out and becomes a little lighter than cool water, so it floats upwards. Cool water at the edges sinks to take its place. Picking 'heavier' is the opposite of what happens.

flow.context: In this step, you watch the loops and time how long one takes.

flow.do: A grown-up switches off the flame. Look at the pan together while the water slows. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: I will switch off the heat. Watch the specks now. Do the loops speed up, slow down or stop?
flow.kid: A grown-up turns off the heat. Watch what the specks do.

ask.q: What happened to the loops when the heat went off?
good: They stopped because the water stopped getting hot at the bottom.

flow.parent: The loops need heat from below to keep going. When it is turned off, the water slowly settles. This is like the Sun: its loops keep going as long as heat comes up from the core.
flow.context: In this step, you switch off the heat and watch the loops slow down.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what I think, what I saw and why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: hot water moves in loops, going up where it is hottest and down where it is cooler. What I saw: the pepper rose in the middle, spread out and sank at the edge, and one loop took about 15 seconds. Why: hot water is lighter, so it floats up, and then cools and sinks. The Sun's outer layer is gas that does the same, and each loop is a granule.
flow.think: A granule on the Sun is about 1,000 kilometres wide and lasts about ten minutes. Why might a bigger loop last longer?
flow.context: In this last step, you say what you found and link it to the Sun.

experiments.title: The Sun's Barcode: split light into colours with a CD
experiments.question: White light is a mix of colours. When you split the light from a torch, a candle and a coloured torch, do they all make the same band of colours?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will a torch, a candle and a red torch all show the same rainbow? If not, how will they be different? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same CD, the same slit and the same distance for every light. Only the light changes, so any difference in the colours comes from the light itself. Look at each light three times, because the colours can be hard to catch on the first try.
results_table: Is the band continuous or in pieces?

materials.item: an old CD or DVD that nobody needs, shiny side showing
a torch with a white light
a piece of red cellophane or red sweet wrapper to cover the torch
a small candle with a safe holder, lit only by a grown-up
2 pieces of black card, each about 10 cm by 10 cm, for the slit
tape and scissors
a dark room

experiments.safety: A grown-up lights and puts out the candle and stays close. Keep the candle on a steel plate away from curtains and hair. Never point the CD, the torch or anything that reflects light at the Sun, and never look at the Sun. Use the torch, the candle and a lamp only. CD edges can be sharp, so a grown-up should handle the edge.

schedule.what: White light is a mix of colours. When you split the light from a torch, a candle and a coloured torch, do they all make the same band of colours?

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the colour band for each light, in order, with the colours you saw.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you use a CD to spread light into its colours. You find out whether every light makes the same rainbow, as a step towards how astronomers read the Sun.

setup.art: Two pieces of black card taped side by side with a thin gap between them, held in front of a torch to make a slit.
setup.caption: 1. Tape two black cards nearly edge to edge to make a thin slit. Hold it in front of the torch.

setup.art: A child in a dark room holding a CD at an angle in front of the slit of light and looking at the colours on the shiny side.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the CD at an angle in the light from the slit. Find the colours on the shiny side.

setup.art: Three drawings of colour bands side by side: a full rainbow for the white torch, a warm band for the candle and a single red band for the red torch.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the band for each light.

flow.do: Show your child the CD, the torch, the candle and the red cellophane. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: We will use a CD to split light into colours. We will look at a white torch, a candle and a red torch. Will they make the same rainbow? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. Will the three lights make the same rainbow? Why?

ask.q: What do you think a red torch will show?
good: The same as the white torch.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sun's Barcode test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Tape two black cards to a torch. 2. Leave a thin gap between them, about as thin as a coin's edge. 3. Make the room dark. 4. Switch on the torch. 5. Stand 2 metres away.
flow.say: Tape two black cards over the torch, nearly touching. Leave a very thin gap between them. This makes a thin line of light, like a slit.
flow.kid: Tape two cards over the torch. Leave a thin gap. Switch it on in the dark.
flow.parent: The slit must be thin, about 1 millimetre. If the line is too wide, the colours smear and you will see only a smudge. Practise holding the torch steady, or rest it on a book.

check.q: Why do we use a thin slit of light?
check.why: A thin line of light gives thin lines of each colour. A wide beam makes every colour overlap and smear. Picking 'to save the battery' is a side effect, not the reason.

flow.context: In this step, you make a thin slit of light, so the colours are sharp.

flow.do: 1. Hold the CD, shiny side towards you, with your arm out and a little tilted. 2. Look at the slit of the white torch in the CD. 3. Tilt the CD slowly until you see a band of colours beside the white line. 4. Write the colours in order. 5. Do it three times.
flow.say: Hold the CD, shiny side to you. Look at the glowing slit in the CD. Tilt it very slowly. Do you see a band of colours? Name them in order.
flow.kid: Hold the CD. Look at the slit in the CD. Tilt it slowly. Find the colours.

ask.q: What colours do you see, and which ones are next to each other?
good: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet.

flow.parent: The colours show only at one tilt, so go slowly. If you see nothing, move closer to the slit or darken the room more. A phone camera can also catch the band if you hold the CD in front of it. Violet may be faint. A white LED torch often shows a strong blue-violet and a gap between green and blue.

check.q: Which colour sits at one end of the band, and which at the other?
options: Red at one end and violet at the other
Red and blue at the same end
All the colours in a muddle
check.why: Light bends by different amounts for different colours, so the band comes out in a fixed order, red at one end and violet at the other. A muddle means the slit is too wide.

flow.context: In this step, you split the white torch's light with the CD.

flow.do: 1. Cover the torch with the red cellophane and look again through the CD. 2. A grown-up lights the candle and puts it behind the slit. 3. Look at the candle's flame in the CD as before. 4. Write the colours you saw for each. 5. A grown-up puts out the candle.
flow.say: Now the red torch. What do you see? Then the candle, lit by a grown-up. How is its band different from the white torch's band?
flow.kid: Look at the red torch. Then the candle. How are the bands different?

ask.q: How are the three bands different?
good: The red torch shows only red.
The candle shows warm colours, red to yellow.
The white torch shows many colours.

flow.parent: The red torch usually shows a single red band, because the cellophane lets only red through. A candle flame shows a continuous band with a lot of orange and yellow, and a little blue. If the candle is too dim, move it close to the slit. The candle's colours are less bright than the torch's, so keep the room very dark.

check.q: Why does the red torch show only red?
options: The cellophane lets through only red light
check.why: The cellophane takes in the other colours and passes the red. Light of one colour makes one band. Picking 'red is the strongest' would not explain why the other colours vanish.

flow.context: In this step, you compare the red torch and the candle with the white torch.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what I think, what I saw and why I think it happened. Then show them the picture of the Sun's spectrum with dark lines.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think the three lights made different bands?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: each kind of light makes its own pattern of colours. What I saw: the white torch showed a wide band from red to violet, the red torch only red, and the candle a warm band. Why: each light is made of different colours. Astronomers do this with the Sun, but with a much finer tool. They see hundreds of thin dark lines, and each kind of atom makes its own pattern. Our CD cannot show those lines, so show the picture of the Sun's spectrum on a phone or in a book.
flow.think: If every atom has its own pattern, how could you tell what a faraway star is made of?
flow.context: In this last step, you say what you found and see how astronomers use it.

activities.title: The Sun in Pictures: what do you notice?

materials.item: a phone, tablet or computer with a picture of the Sun taken by a spacecraft, such as the pictures on NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory website
a sheet of paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Look at pictures of the Sun only on a screen or in a book. Never look at the real Sun.

schedule.what: The Sun in Pictures: what do you notice?

activities.record: Draw the Sun as you saw it in the picture. Write three things you notice, and one question.
activities.context: This is a quick start for the Sun up close. You look at real pictures of the Sun and wonder about its edge, its spots and its glow.

setup.art: A child holding a phone that shows a round picture of the Sun with dark spots and bright loops.
setup.caption: 1. Open a spacecraft picture of the Sun on a screen.

setup.art: A child drawing the Sun on paper, with a ring round it and three notes.
setup.caption: 2. Draw what you see and write three things you notice.

flow.do: Open a recent picture of the Sun taken by a spacecraft. A grown-up can search for the Solar Dynamics Observatory pictures. Look together for one minute without talking.
flow.say: Look at the Sun. Take a whole minute. What do you notice? What do you wonder?
flow.kid: Look at the picture of the Sun. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

ask.q: Is there a sharp edge to the Sun? Is there anything beyond the edge?
good: Yes, there is a round edge.
In some pictures I can see a glow beyond it.

flow.parent: Pictures from space are safe to look at. If the internet is not working, use a book with a picture of the Sun. Different pictures show different layers, so the Sun may look orange, yellow or blue-white. Do not explain yet. Write down what your child notices and wonders.
flow.context: This is a quick start. You look at a real picture of the Sun before anyone explains anything.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the Sun and note three things. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: Draw what you saw. Write three things you noticed. Here is a puzzle. If we flew to the Sun, where would we put our feet?
flow.kid: Draw the Sun. Write three things you noticed. Where would you land?

check.q: If a spacecraft tried to land on the Sun, what would it find?
options: Gas, hotter and thicker the deeper it went
check.why: The Sun is gas from the outside to the centre, getting hotter and thicker as you go in. Picking hot rock is a common thought, because we think of the Sun as a very hot planet.

flow.think: The picture shows a sharp edge. If there is no ground, what is the edge?
flow.context: In this step, you draw the Sun and meet the puzzle this unit will answer.

activities.title: Spin the Orange: how a spot proves the Sun turns

materials.item: 1 orange
3 round stickers or bindis, small
a pencil or a thin skewer to hold the orange, pushed through by a grown-up
a clock or phone with a seconds timer
a table lamp or window light behind you, so the orange is lit from the front

activities.safety: A grown-up pushes the pencil or skewer through the orange. Do not look at the real Sun. Use a lamp or room light.

schedule.what: Spin the Orange: how a spot proves the Sun turns

activities.record: Draw the orange at three positions: spot at the edge coming in, spot in the middle, spot at the edge going out. Write how many seconds the spot was hidden.
activities.context: In this activity, you make a model Sun from an orange and follow a spot as it turns. You find out how a spot crosses, hides and comes back, as in the Kodaikanal story.

setup.art: An orange pushed on a pencil with three round stickers stuck at different places, held up in front of a lamp.
setup.caption: 1. Stick three spots on the orange and hold it by the pencil.

setup.art: A child turning the orange slowly while looking at the front, with arrows showing a spot crossing the face.
setup.caption: 2. Turn the orange steadily. Watch one spot cross.

setup.art: A timer beside the orange, a spot at the far edge and the words 'one second is one day'.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the orange once in 27 seconds. One second stands for one day.

flow.do: Stick one spot at the middle of the orange, one near the top and one low. Ask your child to guess how the spots will move when the orange turns.
flow.say: The orange is our Sun and the stickers are sunspots. When I turn it slowly, what will the middle spot do? What about the spot near the top? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Stick the spots on. Guess how they will move when you turn it.

ask.q: Will all the spots move at the same speed across what you see?
good: The one in the middle will be fastest.
I don't know, they all go round once.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. A grown-up pushes the skewer through the orange from the top to the bottom, so the skewer is the Sun's axis.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Spin the Orange activity. You guess before you turn.

flow.do: 1. Hold the orange at arm's length, facing your child. 2. Turn it slowly to the left and watch one spot. 3. Notice where it looks fastest and where it looks thin and slow. 4. Notice when it vanishes at the edge.
flow.say: Turn the orange slowly. Watch the spot in the middle. Where does it look fastest? Where does it look thin?
flow.kid: Turn the orange slowly. Watch a spot. Where is it fastest? Where is it thin?

ask.q: Where did the spot look thin and squashed?
Why does it look thin there?
good: Because we see it from the side.
It is facing away from us.

flow.parent: Near the edge, the spot is seen from the side, so it looks squashed and it seems to slow down. The spot is really moving at a steady speed. This is the clue Galileo used to show that the spots are on the Sun's surface and not planets in front of it.

check.q: Why does a spot look thin near the Sun's edge?
options: We see it from the side as the ball curves away
check.why: The Sun is a ball, so at the edge the surface is turning away from us. A spot there is seen at a slant, and looks squashed. Picking 'shrinking' is wrong, because the spot is the same size.

flow.context: In this step, you watch how a spot looks as it crosses the front of the orange.

flow.do: 1. Put a spot at the edge where it is about to come into view. 2. Start the timer. 3. Turn the orange steadily so that one full turn takes 27 seconds. 4. Count how many seconds the spot is hidden.
flow.say: Now we use the clock. One second stands for one day. Turn the orange once round in 27 seconds. How long is the spot hidden behind?
flow.kid: Start the timer. Turn the orange once in 27 seconds. How long is the spot hidden?

ask.q: About how long was the spot hidden at the back?
good: About half of 27, so about two weeks.

ask.q: If a spot disappears at the edge, about when will it come back?

flow.parent: A spot is hidden for about half the turn, so about 13 or 14 seconds, standing for about 13 or 14 days. Practise turning at a steady speed. It may take two or three tries. A real spot may also fade while it is hidden, and some never return.

check.q: A sunspot vanishes at the Sun's western edge. About when might it come back?
options: About two weeks later at the eastern edge
The next day at the same edge
check.why: The Sun takes about 27 days to turn once, as seen from the Earth, and a spot is hidden for about half of it. If the spot is still alive, it comes back at the other edge. Picking 'never' is only true if the spot fades while hidden, which we cannot see.

flow.context: In this step, you time how long a spot is hidden, using one second for one day.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what I think, what I saw and why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? Why did the spot go away and come back?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a spot that goes out of sight at one edge goes round the back and can return. What I saw: the spot crossed, looked thin at the edge, hid for about 13 seconds and came back. Why: the orange, like the Sun, is a ball that turns.
flow.think: The Sun is gas, not a solid ball. A spot near its pole takes longer to go round than a spot at its middle. What would the orange need to do to copy that?
flow.context: In this last step, you say what you found.

activities.title: A Stream Past a Stone: how a wind flows round the Earth

materials.item: a large tray, a baking tray or a big steel thali
a jug of water
a small steel katori turned upside down, to be the Earth
a pinch of turmeric or ground pepper
a thick book to tilt the tray
a cloth for spills

activities.safety: Do this at a sink, on a floor that can get wet, or on a balcony. Wipe up spills straight away so nobody slips.

schedule.what: A Stream Past a Stone: how a wind flows round the Earth

activities.record: Draw the tray from above, with the katori and arrows showing how the water flowed round it. Mark where the water was calm behind the katori.
activities.context: In this activity, you make a model of the Sun's wind flowing past the Earth. You see how a stream bends round an obstacle.

setup.art: A tray tilted on a book with an upside-down katori at the centre and a jug of water ready at the high end.
setup.caption: 1. Tilt the tray on a book. Put the katori in the middle.

setup.art: Water with specks of turmeric flowing from the high end, bending round the katori and leaving a calm patch behind it.
setup.caption: 2. Pour gently from the top. Watch the stream bend round the katori.

flow.do: Show your child the tray, the katori and the jug. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: The katori is the Earth, and the water is the wind from the Sun. When I pour water from the top, what will it do when it meets the katori? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. What will the water do when it reaches the katori? Why?

ask.q: What do you think will happen behind the katori?
good: The water will curl round and meet.
There will be a quiet patch.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Stream Past a Stone. You guess before you pour.

flow.do: 1. Tilt the tray on a book. 2. Sprinkle a pinch of turmeric on the high end. 3. Pour water slowly and steadily from the jug at the high end. 4. Watch where the turmeric streams go. 5. Try again, pouring faster.
flow.say: Pour slowly from the top. Watch where the yellow streams go. Where is the water calm? Now pour faster. What changes?
flow.kid: Pour water from the top. Watch the streams. Where is it calm?

ask.q: What shape did the stream make round the katori?
good: It made a tail behind the katori.

ask.q: What changed when you poured faster?
good: The calm patch behind got longer.

flow.parent: The water splits at the front of the katori, flows round both sides and joins up behind it, leaving a calmer tail. The faster the stream, the longer the tail. This is a rough model. The Earth is not a solid thing in the Sun's wind. An invisible magnetic field makes the wind bend, and the field is much wider than the planet.

check.q: What does the katori stand for in this model?
options: The Earth and its magnetic field
check.why: The katori is the obstacle that the stream has to flow round. In real space, the Earth's magnetic field bends the Sun's wind round the planet. Picking the Sun would mix up the stream with the stone.

flow.context: In this step, you pour water and watch how it flows round the katori.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what I think, what I saw and why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think the water bent round the katori?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a stream bends round an obstacle and leaves a calm tail behind. What I saw: the water split in front of the katori, flowed round and left a quiet patch. Why: the stream cannot go through the katori. In space, the Sun's wind flows round the Earth's magnetic field in a similar way. Some of the wind slips in at the poles, and makes the aurora.
flow.think: The real Earth is not solid in the Sun's wind. What part of the Earth is like the katori?
flow.context: In this last step, you say what you found and link it to the Earth.

projects.title: The Sunspot Diary: how long does the Sun take to turn?

materials.item: a phone, tablet or computer with the internet, to see pictures of the Sun from NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory
5 sheets of paper, each with a circle 10 cm wide drawn on it and a straight line through its middle
a ruler and a pencil

projects.safety: Look at pictures of the Sun only on a screen. Never look at the real Sun.

schedule.what: Find a picture with a spot. Copy it on to circle 1 and measure.
Copy the spot on to circle 2.
Copy the spot on to circle 3.
Copy the spot on to circle 4.
Copy the spot on to circle 5. Make the table. Predict the edge.

projects.record: Draw a spot on each sheet and measure its position from the line through the middle. Write the distance it moved each day. Then work out when it will reach the edge.
projects.context: In this project, you follow a real sunspot for five days using pictures from a spacecraft. You work out how fast it moves and when it will reach the edge of the Sun.

setup.art: A phone showing the Sun with a dark spot, beside a sheet of paper with a 10 centimetre circle and a pencil dot where the spot is.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the Sun's picture. Copy the spot on to your circle.

setup.art: Five paper circles in a row, each with the dot a little further across, and a ruler measuring the gap.
setup.caption: 2. Do this for five days. Measure how far the dot moved each day.

flow.do: On day 1, find a recent picture of the Sun with at least one dark spot. Copy the Sun's circle and the spot on to your paper circle. Measure how far the spot is from the line through the middle. Write the date.
flow.say: We will follow a spot for five days. Find a picture with a clear spot, near the middle or at one side. Copy it on to your circle and measure from the middle line. Write the number.
flow.kid: Find a picture with a spot. Copy it on to your circle. Measure its place.

ask.q: Which way do you think the spot will move in the next few days?
good: I think it will go across.

flow.parent: Choose the Solar Dynamics Observatory pictures from the NASA website, and pick the one in white light or orange, where spots show clearly. If there are no spots on the Sun today, use the practice numbers in the project instead: -4.0, -3.2, -2.2, -1.2 and 0.0 centimetres on days 1 to 5. These are made-up practice numbers. Choose the same kind of picture every day, and the same time of day if you can.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Sunspot Diary. You copy a real spot on to your paper.

flow.do: On day 2, find the new picture. Copy the spot on to a new circle. Measure its place and write the date.
flow.say: Day 2. Has the spot moved? Which way? Copy it on to a new circle, measure, and write the number.
flow.kid: Find today's picture. Copy the spot. Measure its place.
flow.parent: Make sure it is the same spot. Spots keep their shape for several days, so you can match them by size and by the spots round them.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Sunspot Diary. You copy the same spot again.

flow.do: On days 3 and 4, do the same. Copy the spot and measure its place on a new circle each day.
flow.say: Days 3 and 4. Keep following your spot. Measure each day. Is it moving the same distance each day?
flow.kid: Copy the spot. Measure its place. Do the same tomorrow.

ask.q: Is the spot moving the same distance every day?
good: It moves a bit less near the edge.

flow.wait: Leave it for two days, and look once each day
flow.context: These are days 3 and 4 of the Sunspot Diary. You keep following the same spot.

flow.do: On day 5, copy the spot for the last time. Make a table of the five places. Find how far it moved each day by taking one place from the next. Find the average. Use it to say when it will reach the edge.
flow.say: Day 5. Let's make a table. How far did the spot move each day? Take away to find out. Then work out how many more days to the edge.
flow.kid: Make a table of the five places. Find how far it moved each day.

ask.q: About how far did the spot move each day when it was near the middle?
When will it reach the edge, at that speed?
good: In about 5 days from the middle.
I divide the distance left by the daily move.

flow.parent: On a 10 centimetre circle, a spot near the middle moves about 1 centimetre a day, and it moves less near the edge because the ball curves away. The whole crossing takes about 13 or 14 days. If your answer is a little different, that is fine. Write down your own number.

check.q: A spot moves about 1 centimetre each day near the middle of a 10 centimetre Sun. About how long would it take to cross from one edge to the other?
check.why: The spot is slower near the edges because the surface curves away. The whole crossing takes about half the Sun's turn, around two weeks. Picking one day mixes up one centimetre with the whole trip.

flow.context: This is day 5 of the Sunspot Diary. You use your numbers to make a prediction.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what I think, what I saw and why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see in your diary? Why did the spot move?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the Sun turns, and the spot is carried across. What I saw: the spot moved about a centimetre a day near the middle. Why: the spot is on the Sun's surface, which turns once in about 27 days as seen from the Earth.
flow.think: If your spot reaches the edge on day 12, when will it come back, if it lasts?
flow.context: In this last step, you say what your diary showed.

challenges.title: The Sun-Facing Stand: find the tilt for solar panels in your city
challenges.problem: A solar panel makes the most electricity when it faces the Sun straight on. Build a card stand that faces the Sun at noon, find its tilt with a protractor, and decide what fixed tilt would be best for your city over the whole year.
constraints: Use only things from home: card, a pencil, clay, a book and a protractor.
Never look at the Sun. Use the shadow of the pencil to aim.
Test between 11 in the morning and 1 in the afternoon, in direct sun.
Write down the tilt you find and the date.
materials: a sheet of stiff card about 15 cm by 20 cm
a straight pencil or a bamboo skewer
a thick book or a box to rest the card on
a sunny balcony, terrace or open window
general: Stick the pencil upright in the middle of the card with clay. Tilt the card until the pencil's shadow shrinks to a dot at its base. Then the card faces the Sun straight on.
Rest the card on a book. Measure the angle between the card and the flat floor with a protractor.
Choose a fixed tilt equal to your city's distance from the equator, called its latitude.
creative: Make a stand with a hinge, so that you can change the tilt for the winter, summer and rainy seasons.
Make a stand with two pencils, so you can see the Sun's east-west direction as well as its height.
Ask a neighbour with solar panels how their panels are tilted and compare with your answer.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own stand. Draw it, build it and test it at noon. What tilt did you find? Is it closer to your city's latitude, or higher, or lower? Why might it change in other months?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about the angle of the Sun. You use a pencil shadow to find the tilt that makes a card face the Sun straight on, and decide what tilt is best for a solar panel.

setup.art: A stiff card with a pencil upright in the middle, tilted so that the pencil's shadow is a dot at its base, resting on a book.
setup.caption: 1. Tilt the card until the pencil's shadow is a dot. The card faces the Sun.

setup.art: A protractor held against the tilted card and the flat floor, showing the angle.
setup.caption: 2. Measure the angle between the card and the floor.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the constraints. Ask your child to draw how they think the card will sit at noon in your city.
flow.say: A solar panel works best when it faces the Sun straight on. At noon, will the card lie flat, lean a little, or stand nearly upright? Draw what you think.
flow.kid: A panel works best facing the Sun. Will the card lie flat or lean? Draw it.

ask.q: In what month and in what city is the card most likely to lie nearly flat?
good: In the middle of the day in summer.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Sun-Facing Stand challenge. You plan and guess.

flow.do: 1. Push the pencil into a lump of clay in the middle of the card, so it stands upright. 2. Take the card out in the sun. 3. Tilt the card slowly until the pencil's shadow becomes a tiny dot at its base. 4. Rest the card on the book and keep it still.
flow.say: Tilt the card slowly. Watch the pencil's shadow. When it shrinks to a dot, the card faces the Sun. Rest it on the book.
flow.kid: Tilt the card. Watch the shadow. Find the tilt that makes a dot.
flow.parent: The shadow dot is the whole trick. Do not look at the Sun. If the card moves, redo it. In November in South India the Sun is fairly low at noon, so the card leans well over, around 25 to 35 degrees. In June it would lean much less.

check.q: When the pencil's shadow is a dot, what does that tell you?
options: The pencil points straight at the Sun
check.why: A pencil makes no shadow only when the Sun is exactly in line with it. The card is square to the pencil, so it also faces the Sun.

flow.context: In this step, you find the tilt that faces the Sun straight on.

flow.do: 1. Hold the protractor against the side of the card and the floor. 2. Read the angle between them. 3. Write it down with the date and time. 4. Look up your city's latitude with a grown-up.
flow.say: Now measure the tilt with the protractor. Write down the angle, the date and the time. What is your city's latitude?
flow.kid: Measure the tilt. Write the angle, the date and the time.

ask.q: Is your tilt bigger or smaller than your city's latitude?

flow.parent: Latitudes are about 10 degrees for Kochi and Madurai, 13 for Chennai, 17 for Hyderabad and 28 for Delhi. Late in the year the Sun is low in the south, so the tilt is larger than the latitude. In midsummer it would be smaller. A fixed panel is usually set to about the city's latitude, facing south, as a compromise for the whole year.
flow.context: In this step, you measure the tilt and compare with your city's latitude.

flow.do: Talk about what you found and what you would change.
flow.say: What tilt did you find? Would it be the same in June? What would you set for a panel that stays fixed all year?
flow.kid: What tilt did you find? Would it be the same in June?

check.q: A panel is fixed in one place all year. Which tilt is a good compromise?
options: About the same as the city's latitude, facing south
check.why: The Sun's height changes through the year, higher in summer and lower in winter. A tilt close to the latitude is right half-way between. Flat or upright would be good for only a few days.

flow.context: In this last step, you decide on a tilt for the whole year.

items.p: Put the Sun's layers in order, from the inside out.
items.why: Energy is made in the core, then crosses the radiative zone and the boiling convection zone. The photosphere is the layer we call the surface, and above it lie the thin chromosphere and the huge corona.

items.p: What is the photosphere?
opts: The layer where the Sun's gas becomes clear enough for light to escape
A solid crust over the Sun
items.why: The photosphere is the layer we see as the Sun's surface. It is not a crust. Below it the gas is too thick for light to get out. Picking 'a solid crust' is common, because we draw the Sun with a skin.

items.p: The Sun's outer atmosphere, which is hotter than its surface, is called the ____.
items.why: The corona is over a million degrees Celsius, much hotter than the 5,500 degrees of the photosphere below it.

items.p: You could stand on the Sun's surface if you wore a suit that could survive the heat.
items.why: False. The Sun is gas from the outside to the centre, so there is no solid ground to stand on. A spacecraft would sink through thinner and then thicker gas.

items.p: Imagine a jar of water with a little milk in it, lit from below. Explain why the cloud seems to have a glowing edge, even though you could put your hand into it.
items.a: The milk scatters light, so you can only see a short way into the cloud. Light from deeper down does not reach your eyes. The edge you see is just how far you can see, and not a wall.
items.why: A strong answer says that the edge is where we stop being able to see in. The Sun's surface works in the same way.

items.p: A sunspot looks dark. What is the best reason?
opts: It is cooler than the gas around it
It is a hole in the Sun
It is a planet in front of the Sun
It has no light at all
items.why: A sunspot is about 4,000 degrees Celsius, cooler than the 5,500 degrees around it. Next to the brighter Sun it looks dark, but alone it would glow brightly. A hole or a planet would not behave like a spot.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: a bubble of hot gas about 1,000 kilometres wide at the Sun's surface
a cooler patch held by a strong magnetic field
a stream of charged pieces flowing out from the corona
glowing light near the poles when charged pieces hit the Earth's air
hot material rising and cooler material sinking in a loop
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These words are the main ideas of the unit. A strong answer could give an example of each.

items.p: A sunspot crosses the Sun and vanishes at the western edge. About when might it come back?
opts: About two weeks later at the eastern edge
The next morning at the same edge
items.why: The Sun turns once in about 27 days as seen from the Earth. The spot is hidden for about half of that. If it is still alive, it comes back at the eastern edge.

items.p: Draw the Sun three times. In the first, show a spot just arriving at one edge. In the second, show it in the middle. In the third, show it leaving at the other edge. Draw how its shape changes.
items.a: Three circles with a spot. At the edge the spot is thin and squashed. In the middle it is round. At the other edge it is thin again.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the squashed edge shape. It tells us that the Sun is a ball and the spot is on its surface.
items.art: Three blank circles in a row, each with a vertical line through the middle.

items.p: Label the cut-open Sun: core, convection zone, photosphere and corona.
items.a: The core in the middle, the convection zone as a layer in the outer part, the photosphere at the bright edge, and the corona as a faint glow outside the edge.
items.why: The layers go from the hot core outwards to the thin corona. A strong label puts the corona outside the bright edge.
items.art: A circle cut in half with four blank label lines pointing to the centre, the outer layer, the edge and the glow outside.

items.p: Sort these into things from a flare and things from the solar wind.
items: a flash of light that reaches the Earth in about 8 minutes
a steady stream of charged pieces that flows past the Earth
a burst set off by the snap of a magnetic field above sunspots
a flow that pushes comet tails away from the Sun
a flow that takes a few days to reach the Earth
items.a: see items
items.why: A flare is a sudden event with a flash of light. The wind is a steady stream that never stops. A strong answer uses speed and steadiness to tell them apart.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Sunspots, flares and granules all happen on or just above the Sun. An aurora happens in the Earth's air, high above the ground, when charged pieces from the Sun hit it.

items.p: Why do we see only the photosphere in an ordinary picture of the Sun?
opts: Light from deeper down cannot escape the thick gas
The deeper layers are cold and dark
The camera is not good enough
items.why: The gas below the photosphere is so thick that light is taken in and sent out again after a very short distance. Only light from the photosphere and above can get out into space.

items.p: Two friends are talking about the Sun.

views.says: The Sun has a surface, like the Earth, and I can see its edge in every picture.
The Sun has no ground. What we see as the edge is just where we stop being able to see in.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use the idea of how deep you can see into a cloud. Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer sides with Rafiq: the Sun is gas, and the photosphere is the layer where light can escape, so the sharp edge shows how far we can see. It also gives Divya her due: the edge in the picture is real to our eyes and is a good place to call the surface.
items.why: This tests the main idea: the edge of the Sun is where we stop seeing in, not a wall.

items.p: A pan of water on a low flame shows specks rising in the middle and sinking at the edge. Explain why this helps us to understand the Sun's surface.
items.a: Hot water is lighter and rises, then cools and sinks, so it goes round in loops. The Sun's outer layer is hot gas that boils in the same way, with bright bubbles rising and cooler gas sinking in the lanes between them.
items.why: A strong answer names hot rising, cool sinking and a loop, and links it to granules.

items.p: The dark lines in sunlight's rainbow tell us which atoms are in the Sun.
items.why: True. Each kind of atom takes out its own pattern of colours. The same patterns are made by those atoms in laboratories on Earth.

items.p: The Sun's wind blows past the Earth. What does this tell us?
opts: The Earth is inside the Sun's outer atmosphere
The Earth is part of the Sun's core
Space is full of air like on Earth
The wind is too weak to matter
items.why: The solar wind fills the solar system, so the Earth sits inside the Sun's thin outer gas. It does not mean space has air like ours. The wind is very thin.

items.p: A sunspot near the Sun's middle goes round in about 25 days, and a spot near the pole takes about 35 days. What does this tell us?
opts: The Sun is a ball of gas, not a solid ball
The Sun has a crack in it
items.why: A solid ball turns all in one piece, so every spot would take the same time. Different times in different places mean the Sun is gas, which can turn at different speeds.

items.p: Use the idea of a spinning orange to explain why a sunspot looks thin and squashed near the Sun's edge.
items.a: The Sun is a ball, so near the edge the surface curves away from us. We see the spot at a slant, so it looks thin and seems to move slowly, even though it moves at a steady speed.
items.why: A strong answer says the Sun is a ball and the spot is seen from the side at the edge. It also says the spot has not shrunk.

items.p: Heinrich Schwabe, a pharmacist, drew the Sun for many years and found that the number of sunspots rises and falls in a cycle of about ____ years.
items.why: The average cycle is about 11 years, though a cycle can be shorter or longer. Schwabe first saw it as about ten years.

items.p: A flare and a cloud of plasma leave the Sun at the same time. Which arrives first, and about when?
opts: The flash of light, in about 8 minutes
items.why: Light travels at the greatest speed there is. A cloud of plasma is made of material, so it is much slower and takes one to three days.

items.p: Put these in order, from the one that takes the least time to reach the Earth to the one that takes the most.
items: wind that leaves the Sun at an ordinary speed
a cloud of plasma from a big eruption
the first particles of a flare
a: the first particles of a flare
a cloud of plasma from a big eruption
wind that leaves the Sun at an ordinary speed
items.why: Light takes about 8 minutes. Some fast particles arrive in an hour or so. A fast eruption cloud takes a day or two. The ordinary wind takes about four days. A strong answer uses the word 'speed'.

items.p: Label the picture of the Earth in the Sun's wind: the Sun, the wind, the Earth's magnetic field and the aurora.
items.a: The Sun on one side, arrows of wind coming towards the Earth, the field bending the wind round the Earth, and glowing light at the poles.
items.why: The field steers the wind round the Earth and down towards the poles. A strong label puts the aurora at the poles.
items.art: The Sun on the left, arrows streaming right, and a small Earth with curved field lines round it and four blank label lines.

items.p: Why does an aurora appear near the poles and not at the equator?
opts: The Earth's magnetic field steers the charged pieces towards the poles
The poles are closer to the Sun
items.why: The magnetic field lines of the Earth go into the ground near the poles, and charged pieces follow them down. In a very strong storm the aurora can reach farther from the poles.

items.p: Solar storms are the main reason it rains more in some years.
items.why: False. Space storms affect satellites, radio and power lines. The Sun's total light changes very little over the cycle, too little to explain big changes in rain.

items.p: Sort each thing into 'can be harmed by a strong space storm' or 'not affected much'.
items: a GPS guide on a phone
items.a: see items
items.why: Storms disturb electronics, radio and long metal lines. Ordinary things with no electronics or long wires are hardly affected. A strong answer talks about electric current and radio signals.

items.p: A coil heater glows dull red, then orange as it gets hotter. What does a blue-white star tell you?
opts: It is hotter than a red star
It is colder than a red star
It is the same as a red star
items.why: Hotter things glow bluer and whiter, and cooler things glow redder. A star's colour is a clue to its temperature.

items.p: Fraunhofer saw hundreds of dark lines in sunlight's rainbow, and Kirchhoff and Bunsen showed that sodium makes a pair of lines in the same place. What did this tell them about the Sun?
items.a: The dark lines come from atoms in the Sun's outer layers taking out their own colours. Sodium makes a pair of lines, so sodium atoms are in the Sun.
items.why: A strong answer says each atom has its own pattern and the match means that atom is present.

items.p: Two friends are talking about the corona being hotter than the Sun's surface.

views.says: It is hotter because waves from the surface carry energy up and heat it.
It is hotter because there are millions of tiny flares up there, and each one gives a little heat.

items.ask: Which idea do you find more convincing? What would you want to measure to find out? Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer admits that scientists do not yet know. It names a test, such as measuring waves in the corona, or counting tiny flares with spacecraft. It gives both friends their due, since both processes may share the work.
items.why: This tests how scientists treat an open puzzle: they list ideas and plan measurements.

items.p: Why does the corona have less heat than the surface even though its temperature is higher?
opts: It is very thin, so it holds little material to hold heat
It is closer to the core
It is colder than the surface
items.why: Temperature is how fast the particles move. Heat also depends on how many particles there are. The corona has very few, so it holds little heat, like a hot spark.

items.p: Draw the Sun with its wind. Show three arrows of wind going out, and draw the Earth with a bubble of the Sun's wind round it.
items.a: A circle for the Sun, arrows going out in all directions, and the Earth inside a large bubble of wind.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the Earth inside the wind and not outside it.
items.art: A circle for the Sun on the left and a blank space to the right.

items.p: Four people studied the Sun. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Fraunhofer, Kirchhoff and Bunsen worked on the Sun's rainbow of colours and its dark lines. Galileo used a telescope to show sunspots, and lived much earlier.

items.p: Which tells us the most about what a faraway star is made of?
opts: The dark lines in its rainbow of colours
items.why: Each kind of atom takes out its own pattern of colours, so the lines give the star's ingredients. Size or twinkling does not.

items.p: Christoph Scheiner thought sunspots were small planets near the Sun. Which clue best shows he was wrong?
opts: Spots look thin near the edge and cross the Sun at different speeds, which small planets in orbit would not do
items.why: A small orbiting planet would move at a steady speed and keep its shape. Spots slow down and thin out near the edge, and change shape, because they are on a turning ball.

items.p: Parker said that the corona is too hot to stay still, and must flow outwards as a wind. Why would very hot gas not stay still around the Sun?
items.a: Hot gas has fast-moving particles, and the Sun's pull cannot hold them all. Some escape and stream away, so the gas flows out like a wind.
items.why: A strong answer says the hot gas's particles move fast enough to escape the Sun's pull.

items.p: A comet is leaving the Sun, and its tail still points away from the Sun. What does this show?
opts: The tail is pushed by the Sun's wind and light, not left behind by the comet's movement
The tail is made of fire
items.why: If the tail were only left behind, it would point back along the comet's path. A tail pointing away from the Sun, even when the comet is leaving it, shows that something from the Sun pushes it.

items.p: A friend says, 'The Sun's edge is a wall, and space starts there.' Use two facts from this unit to answer them.
items.a: The Sun is gas, so there is no wall. The edge is the layer where light can escape. The corona and the wind continue beyond it and blow past the Earth, so space near us still has the Sun's gas in it.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea of the photosphere and the wind to show that the Sun does not stop at the edge.

items.p: A class is deciding how to watch the Sun's spots.

views.says: We should look at pictures from a spacecraft, because they are safe and clear.
We should make our own pictures with a projection, because we learn more by doing it ourselves.

items.ask: Which plan would you choose, and why? Then say one good thing about the other plan.
items.a: A strong answer picks one and gives a reason. It gives credit to the other: spacecraft pictures are clear and safe, while a home projection shows the real Sun today and teaches how people first saw spots. Neither involves looking at the Sun directly.
items.why: There is a real trade-off between quality and learning by doing. Both are safe.

items.p: A scientist measures the rotation of the Sun by following one spot for 5 days. Give two reasons why the answer is less exact than it seems.
items.a: Spots at different latitudes move at different speeds, so a spot's speed depends on where it is. Spots also grow, shrink and fade while you watch, so the same spot is hard to follow.
items.why: A strong answer gives two reasons, one about different speeds and one about spots changing.

items.p: Put these steps in order for how an eruption on the Sun affects the Earth.
items: The cloud pushes on the Earth's magnetic field and an aurora glows
A cloud of plasma crosses space in a day or more
Light and X-rays reach the Earth in about 8 minutes
Magnetic field above sunspots snaps and a flare flashes
a: Magnetic field above sunspots snaps and a flare flashes
Light and X-rays reach the Earth in about 8 minutes
A cloud of plasma crosses space in a day or more
The cloud pushes on the Earth's magnetic field and an aurora glows
items.why: The flare comes first and its light reaches the Earth fast. The slower cloud follows. When it hits, the Earth's field is shaken and the aurora glows. A strong answer uses speed to order the steps.

items.p: An astronomer sees a gap between two colours in a star's rainbow where the colour is missing. What could have caused it?
items.a: Atoms in the star's outer layers took in light of that colour. Each kind of atom takes out its own colours, so the gap is a clue to which atom is there.
items.why: A strong answer names atoms taking in light and links the missing colour to a kind of atom.

items.p: The corona is hotter than the Sun's surface. Which would be the best way to test the idea of nanoflares?
opts: Count tiny bright flashes in the corona with a spacecraft
items.why: If many tiny flares heat the corona, then we should see many small flashes. A spacecraft that can see the corona closely can count them. Looking at the Moon or the stars tells us nothing about it.

items.p: If the Sun's magnetic field vanished tomorrow, there would be no sunspots.
items.why: True. Sunspots are patches where strong magnetic fields slow the boiling gas and keep it cooler. Without the field, there would be nothing to make them.

items.p: Label the sunspot cycle graph: a peak, a valley and the time between two peaks.
items.a: A high point labelled maximum, a low point labelled minimum, and about 11 years between two peaks.
items.why: The cycle swings between busy and quiet. A strong label gives about 11 years.
items.art: A wavy line graph with a peak, a valley and two blank label lines.

items.p: Aditya-L1 sits near a point called L1, about 1.5 million kilometres from the Earth. Why is that a good place to watch the Sun?
opts: The Earth never blocks its view of the Sun
It is close to the Moon
items.why: From a spot between the Earth and the Sun, the Earth never gets in the way, so the Sun can be watched all the time.

items.p: Why might a space storm bring both beautiful aurora and trouble for a power company?
items.a: Both come from the same cause: charged pieces and changing magnetic fields arrive at the Earth. The glow is light made high in the air. The changing field can push extra current along long power lines.
items.why: A strong answer says one cause, the storm, has both a beautiful and a harmful result.

items.p: Draw a timeline of what the Sun sends to the Earth after a big eruption. Mark 8 minutes, 1 day and 4 days.
items.a: A line with a flash at 8 minutes, a fast cloud near 1 to 3 days, and ordinary wind at about 4 days.
items.why: A strong drawing orders the three arrivals by speed.
items.art: A blank horizontal line with a Sun at the left end and an Earth at the right end.

items.p: Which statement is the most honest about forecasting space weather?
opts: We can give some warning of big storms but cannot say exactly which will hit or when
We can forecast it as exactly as rain
We cannot forecast it at all
items.why: Scientists can watch eruptions leave the Sun and track clouds, but they cannot yet predict exactly when a storm will start or how strong it will be at the Earth.

items.p: Tiny particles in air or in milky water scatter ____ light sideways more than red light.
items.why: Blue light is scattered more, so the sky and the side of the milky jar look bluish. Light that goes straight on loses its blue and looks orange or red.

opts: The layer where the Sun's gas becomes clear enough for light to escape
quiz.why: The photosphere is the layer we see as the Sun's surface. Below it, the gas is too thick for light to escape. Picking a solid crust is the most common mistake.

quiz.p: Which is the correct order of layers, from the core outwards?
opts: Core, radiative zone, convection zone, photosphere, chromosphere, corona
quiz.why: Energy is made in the core and moves outwards through the layers. The corona is the outermost.

quiz.p: Why does a sunspot look dark?
opts: It is cooler than the gas around it
quiz.why: A sunspot is still hot, about 4,000 degrees Celsius, but it is cooler than the 5,500 degrees round it, so it looks dark by comparison.

quiz.p: A sunspot disappears at one edge of the Sun. What is the best explanation?
opts: The Sun turns, so the spot has gone round the back
quiz.why: The Sun turns like a ball. A spot that crosses to the edge is carried round the far side and can return about two weeks later.

quiz.p: A spot near the Sun's pole takes longer to go round than a spot near the middle. What does that show?
opts: The Sun is gas and turns at different speeds
quiz.why: A solid ball turns in one piece. The Sun does not, so it must be gas.

opts: A steady stream of charged pieces flowing out from the Sun's corona
quiz.why: The solar wind is made of charged pieces, not air. It flows out in all directions and passes the Earth at about 400 kilometres in every second.

quiz.p: What does it mean that the Earth is inside the Sun's atmosphere?
opts: The Sun's thin outer gas and wind reach past the Earth
The Earth is part of the Sun
quiz.why: The Sun's wind fills the space round all the planets. We are inside it, just as a fish is inside a lake.

quiz.p: Why does an aurora glow near the poles?
opts: The Earth's magnetic field steers charged pieces towards the poles
quiz.why: Charged pieces follow the magnetic field lines down at the poles and make the gases glow.

quiz.p: How long does a flare's flash take to reach the Earth?
quiz.why: A flash of light moves at the speed of light and takes about 8 minutes. The slower cloud takes a day or more.

quiz.p: Why is Aditya-L1 placed near a point called L1?
opts: From there, the Earth never blocks its view of the Sun
It is the closest place to the Sun
It is safe from all storms
It is where the Moon is
quiz.why: L1 is on the Sun's side of the Earth, about 1.5 million kilometres away, so the Sun can be watched without a break.

quiz.p: What do the dark lines in the Sun's rainbow tell us?
opts: Which kinds of atom are in the Sun
quiz.why: Each kind of atom takes out its own pattern of colours. The lines match the patterns made by those atoms in laboratories.

quiz.p: Comet tails always point away from the Sun. What did this help scientists to guess?
opts: Something flows out from the Sun and pushes the tails
The tail is made of rock
quiz.why: Ludwig Biermann used this clue in 1951 to say that a stream must flow out from the Sun. Parker explained the stream in 1958 and Mariner 2 measured it in 1962.

open_questions.q: Why is the Sun's corona so much hotter than its surface?
open_questions.why_open: Two main ideas exist, heating by waves and heating by countless tiny flares. Spacecraft such as Parker Solar Probe and Aditya-L1 are collecting data, but scientists have not decided.

open_questions.q: Can we predict when a big solar storm will hit the Earth, a week before?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can watch eruptions leave the Sun, but they cannot yet say reliably which sunspot group will erupt, or how strong the storm will be at the Earth.

open_questions.q: Why does the Sun's magnetic field flip about every 11 years?
open_questions.why_open: Computer models of the Sun's magnetism give cycles, but they do not agree on every detail, and some cycles come out stronger than the models expect.

open_questions.q: Where does the Sun's wind end and space between the stars begin?
open_questions.why_open: Voyager 1 left the Sun's wind bubble in 2012, according to NASA, but the shape and size of the whole bubble are still being worked out.

open_questions.q: Was the Sun brighter or fainter when it was young?
open_questions.why_open: Many scientists think the young Sun was about a quarter to a third fainter, yet the early Earth had liquid water. How that was possible is still debated.

open_questions.q: Are there sunspots on other stars?
open_questions.why_open: Astronomers have seen signs of huge starspots on some stars, but starspots are hard to see, because other stars look like single points of light.

maths.problem: A granule on the Sun's surface is about 1,000 kilometres wide. The Earth is about 12,700 kilometres wide. About how many granules would fit across the Earth?
maths.explain: 12,700 divided by 1,000 is 12.7. That is a little under 13, so about 13 granules would fit in a line across the Earth.
maths.why_maths: Comparing a small bubble on the Sun with the Earth gives a feel for how big even the Sun's smallest features are.

maths.problem: A sunspot moves about 1 centimetre each day across a 10 centimetre picture of the Sun, when it is near the middle. It is now at the middle. About how many days until it is at the edge, 5 centimetres away?
maths.answer: About 5 days, a little more because it slows near the edge.
maths.explain: 5 centimetres divided by 1 centimetre a day is 5 days. Near the edge the spot looks slower, because the ball curves away, so it takes a little longer than 5 days.
maths.context: In the Sunspot Diary, you copy a real spot on to paper each day and measure how far it moved.
maths.why_maths: Dividing a distance by a daily step is how you predict when something will arrive.

maths.problem: The solar wind travels at about 400 kilometres in every second. The Sun is about 150 million kilometres away. How many seconds does it take to reach the Earth, and about how many days is that? A day has 86,400 seconds.
maths.answer: About 375,000 seconds, which is a little over 4 days.
maths.explain: 150,000,000 divided by 400 is 375,000 seconds. 375,000 divided by 86,400 is about 4.3. So the wind takes a little over 4 days.
maths.why_maths: The wind is slower than light. Dividing the distance by its speed shows how long it takes, so we can predict when a storm arrives.

maths.problem: Light from the Sun takes 8 minutes to reach the Earth. The wind takes about 4 days. A day has 24 hours and an hour has 60 minutes. How many times as long does the wind take?
maths.explain: 4 days is 4 times 24 hours, which is 96 hours. 96 hours is 96 times 60 minutes, which is 5,760 minutes. 5,760 divided by 8 is 720.
maths.why_maths: Changing both times into minutes lets us compare them with one division.

maths.problem: Suppose the number of sunspots was highest in the year 2000. The cycle lasts 11 years. In which years will the next three highs come?
maths.explain: 2000 plus 11 is 2011. 2011 plus 11 is 2022. 2022 plus 11 is 2033. The pattern adds 11 each time.
maths.why_maths: A cycle is a repeating pattern, and adding the same step each time lets us look ahead.

maths.problem: At the Sun's middle, one turn takes about 25 days. Near a pole it takes about 35 days. How many whole turns will each make in 100 days?
maths.answer: Four turns at the middle, and two whole turns near a pole.
maths.explain: 100 divided by 25 is exactly 4. 100 divided by 35 is 2 with 30 left over, so two whole turns and most of a third.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the time by the turn time shows how much the two speeds differ, a clue that the Sun is gas.

maths.problem: A card faces the Sun straight on when the pencil on it casts no shadow. Its tilt from the flat floor is 29 degrees. The Sun's height above the horizon is the rest of the way to a right angle, 90 degrees. How high is the Sun?
maths.explain: The card and the pencil make a right angle. The card tilts 29 degrees from flat, so the Sun is 90 take away 29, which is 61 degrees above the horizon.
maths.context: In the Sun-Facing Stand challenge, you tilt a card until the pencil's shadow is a dot, then measure the tilt with a protractor.
maths.why_maths: A right angle is 90 degrees, so knowing one angle gives the other. This is how we find the Sun's height from a tilt.

maths.problem: In the Glowing Fog test, these were the depths where a black patch vanished: 9 centimetres, 6 centimetres, 3 centimetres, 2 centimetres, 1 centimetre. The milk doubled each time. Between which two steps did the depth fall most? How much?
maths.answer: Between the first and second, and the second and third, it fell 3 centimetres each time.
maths.explain: 9 take away 6 is 3. 6 take away 3 is 3. 3 take away 2 is 1. 2 take away 1 is 1. The biggest falls were 3 centimetres, at the first two steps.
maths.context: In the Glowing Fog test, you add milk to a jar of water and find the depth where a black patch vanishes. These numbers are made up.
maths.why_maths: Looking at the changes between steps shows where the milk had the most effect, which is what a line graph would show.

maths.problem: In the Boiling Pot, one speck takes 15 seconds to go round one loop. How many loops would it make in 2 minutes?
maths.explain: 2 minutes is 120 seconds. 120 divided by 15 is 8.
maths.context: In the Boiling Pot, you watch pepper specks go round in loops and time one loop.
maths.why_maths: Changing minutes to seconds and dividing shows how often a loop repeats, like the Sun's granules.
